thread.title: Micron Technology: Where Are The Demand Drivers? - SK Hynix, Inc. (OTCMKTS:HXSCL)

author: Robert Castellano
title: Micron Technology: Where Are The Demand Drivers? - SK Hynix, Inc. (OTCMKTS:HXSCL)
text:
Since the beginning of 2019, the memory market has been hit with a significant amount of negative news.
On Jan. 15, DRAM manufacturer Nanya Technology ( OTCPK:NNYAF ) reported its Q4 2018 revenue was $551 million, down 30.4% QoQ. On Jan. 24, 2019, SK Hynix ( OTC:HXSCL ) reported Q4 2018 earnings. Revenues fell 13.7% QoQ to $8.7 billion, while operating profit amounted to $3.9 billion, down 32.4%. SK’s DRAM and NAND bit shipments dropped 2.5% and rose 10% QoQ, respectively, while its DRAM and NAND ASPs fell 11.1% and 21.2% QoQ, respectively. Also on Jan. 24, Western Digital ( WDC ) reported revenue of $4.2 billion for its second fiscal quarter ended Dec. 28, 2018, down 20.7% QoQ. Operating income was $176 million with a net loss of $487 million. On Jan. 31, 2019, Samsung Electronics ( OTC:SSNLF ) reported Q4 2018 DRAM and NAND revenues of $18.8 billion and $6.6 billion in operating profit, down 27.7% and 43.0% QoQ, respectively. Samsung’s DRAM and NAND bit shipments were down 18.3% and 9.7% QoQ, respectively, while ASPs were down 9.7% and 21.5% QoQ, respectively. DRAMeXchange reported on Feb. 1, 2019 that memory semiconductor prices plunged in January of this year. The price of DRAM chips showed a 17.2% drop, the biggest in four years, while that of NAND flash decreased by 3%. Bit Growth in 2019 Micron ( MU ) revised down its DRAM and NAND bit growth forecasts for this year to 16% and 35% (from 20% and 40%). SK Hynix’ guidance for DRAM and NAND bit growth this year is for percentages in the high teens and 30s, respectively. Samsung Electronics expects DRAM and NAND bit demand in 2019 to grow 16-19% and 34-36%, respectively. Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology can resort to the price control strategy because they are oligopolistic players in the global DRAM market. Their combined market share amounted to 95.5 percent in Q4 2018. They will keep their production volume below their bit shipments to reduce inventory. If demand turns out weaker than expected, the firms could consider cutting investments further.

Investor Takeaway The memory market has been in slowdown mode for the last three months, as reflected in poor financial reports by Samsung, SK Hynix, Western Digital, and Nanya, which I illustrated in this article. Q4 2018 financials were down nearly across the board, and this negative trend is projected to continue through Q1 2019.
However, while guidance from the memory makers is pointing to the trough ending in Q3, this is speculation because there are uncertainties in interpreting the cause of the slowdown across all client end-use applications.
A significant factor is the current trade dispute, which is impacting the overall macroeconomic economies of not only China and the U.S. but all global economies. But the depth and breadth of the trade dispute remains unknown. Indeed, the smartphone market probably dropped 4% in 2018, but memory content per phone increased. But how much of the drop is attributed to a global slowdown and how much from smartphones that don't offer a real incentive to upgrade? And did the memory companies shoot themselves in the foot by allowing ASPs to rise resulting in a rise in the price of phones and a drop in demand? These are unknown factors that contribute to uncertainties in predicting an upturn.
A slowdown in China may impact smartphone supplier Apple ( AAPL ), but there are factors that may have to do with Apple’s marketing in China (e.g., high prices) than with the China trade war in itself.
Another excuse for the slowdown in memory were Intel’s (NASDAQ: INTC ) CPU shortages, which affected PC supply. Upon closer analysis of the CPU market, however, PC shipments increased 4.5% in 2018 following only a 1.7% YoY growth in 2017.
Rumors persist of data center delays in placing new DRAM and NAND orders. But further analysis shows that it has been excess memory inventories that were responsible, and when inventory adjustments are made the server market will resume its rampant growth. In other words, data centers did not cut back on memory purchases because of problems at data centers, but because they were using up inventories and delaying purchases as memory ASPs continue to decline. The tide has turned, and it's now a buyer's market.
Memory companies are countering. Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology can resort to the price control strategy because they are oligopolistic players in the global DRAM market. Their combined market share amounted to 95.5 percent in Q4 2018. They will keep their production volume below their bit shipments to reduce inventory. If demand turns out weaker than expected, the firms could consider cutting investments further.
Table 1 illustrates the changes in capex spending based on supplier guidance. These significant cuts will impact the processing equipment suppliers, particularly Lam Research (NASDAQ: LRCX ) and Applied Materials (NASDAQ: AMAT ).
